issues.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference when a party withholds important, relevant documents in that party’s possession, even if the burden of proof does not rest on that party and production was not expressly demanded.
material_facts: The dispute concerned ownership of land associated with a public religious trust.
The claimant, who managed the trust and admitted possessing separate accounts of its income, did not produce those accounts or his own accounts showing how income from the land was dealt with.
The accounts could have shed light on whether the land and its income belonged to the trust or to the claimant.
issues.conclusion: The court may draw an adverse inference against a party who withholds important documents in that party’s possession, notwithstanding the allocation of the burden of proof or the absence of an express demand for production.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 114, illustration (g), of the Evidence Act, a court may infer that withheld evidence would be unfavorable to the person withholding it. The court applied Murugesam Pillai v. Manickavasaka Pandara and Biltu Ram v. Jainandan Prasad, and explained that Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh does not bar such an inference merely because a demand for production was not made.

rule.if: civil_property_dispute and important_records_in_party_possession and records_relevant_to_dispute and party_withheld_records

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The proceeding involves a dispute over ownership or rights in property.
predicates.important_records_in_party_possession: A party possesses important records that could assist in deciding the dispute.
predicates.records_relevant_to_dispute: The records could shed light on a fact in issue.
predicates.party_withheld_records: The party did not produce the relevant records to the court.

issues.definition: When a property dispute involves important, relevant records in a party’s possession and that party withholds them, an adverse inference is permitted.

issues.legal_issue: Land associated with a public religious trust belongs to the trust where the evidence supports the trust’s ownership and the claimed private ownership is not substantiated.
material_facts: The disputed land included the site of a long-established shrine and was associated with public facilities and burials near the shrine.
The claimant’s family managed the shrine and possessed the land in that managerial capacity.
An old survey record did not name the claimant’s family, and the claimant produced no grant or other documentary evidence showing how the family acquired title.
Later records naming members of the family as occupants or holders were consistent with their management and possession on behalf of the shrine.
The claimant admitted receiving income from the land and possessing separate accounts of the shrine’s income but did not produce the accounts showing how the income was dealt with.
issues.conclusion: The disputed land belonged to the public trust and was properly shown as its property.
issues.legal_principle: The court assessed the documentary and circumstantial evidence of title and possession, including the absence of an early record or title document supporting private ownership and the explanation that later entries reflected fiduciary management. It also applied section 114, illustration (g), of the Evidence Act to the withheld accounts, relying on Murugesam Pillai v. Manickavasaka Pandara and Biltu Ram v. Jainandan Prasad; it distinguished Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh as not preventing an adverse inference where documents were not expressly demanded.

rule.if: civil_trust_property_appeal and land_associated_with_public_shrine and family_possession_as_manager and old_record_omits_claimed_owner and no_title_document_produced and later_entries_consistent_with_management and relevant_income_accounts_withheld

predicates.civil_trust_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil dispute over whether property belongs to a public trust.
predicates.land_associated_with_public_shrine: The disputed land includes or is associated with a public religious shrine.
predicates.family_possession_as_manager: The claimant’s family possessed or managed the property in a fiduciary capacity for the shrine.
predicates.old_record_omits_claimed_owner: An early record concerning the land does not name the person or family claiming private ownership.
predicates.no_title_document_produced: The claimant produces no grant or other documentary evidence establishing how private title was acquired.
predicates.later_entries_consistent_with_management: Later records naming the claimant’s family as occupants or holders are consistent with their management of the trust property rather than private ownership.
predicates.relevant_income_accounts_withheld: The claimant possesses but does not produce accounts that could show how income from the property was handled.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns trust property associated with a public shrine, and managerial possession, the documentary history, and withheld relevant income accounts support trust ownership, the trust owns the disputed land.
